cases.summary: In Kiket Island, Swinomish Reservation, Washington, Swinomish Kiket Island Clam Garden is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program uses community-based biocultural clam-garden restoration using rock-terrace construction and tending. The project responds to sea-level rise and ocean acidification. Available materials report that construction began and long-term monitoring initiated. The available materials do not identify a measured project outcome. The case is presented as an implementation example, not as evidence that the same results will occur in another place or under different conditions.
cases.title: Swinomish Kiket Island Clam Garden

cases.asset_alt: Tulalip Natural Resources image showing the top of a beaver lodge in a wetland habitat.
cases.summary: In Upper Snohomish / Skykomish watershed, Washington, Tulalip Beaver Relocation is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The documented approach is to relocate nuisance beavers from developed areas to hydrologically impaired tributaries or public land to support fish habitat and water storage. The cited material connects the relocation work to warming and drying climate. Historical relocation and wildlife-camera monitoring are documented. The available materials do not identify an independent measured project outcome.
cases.title: Tulalip Beaver Relocation

cases.asset_alt: A resident standing in front of a RainWise rain garden at a Seattle home.
cases.summary: In Seattle, Washington, Seattle RainWise Residential Stormwater Retrofits is an implementation initiative. The program uses rebates and approved-contractor support for rain gardens and cisterns on eligible private properties. Heavy rainfall and stormwater entering combined sewer infrastructure can contribute to polluted overflows. The available materials describe the program and its implementation status but do not report an outcome. The source documents the action and its implementation context. It does not by itself establish broader effectiveness or outcomes beyond the reported evidence.
cases.title: Seattle RainWise Residential Stormwater Retrofits

cases.summary: In Taholah, Quinault Indian Nation, Washington, Quinault Taholah Village Relocation is an implementation initiative. The documented approach is to plan phased relocation of Taholah Village to higher ground to address coastal and river-flooding risks. The case addresses coastal/river flooding and storm-surge exposure. Available materials report master-plan adoption and phased relocation planning. The available materials do not identify a measured relocation outcome.
cases.title: Quinault Taholah Village Relocation

The program uses site-specific dynamic revetment using cobble/rocks, with monitoring and adaptive management. The case addresses bounded coastal erosion/flooding exposure and shoreline adaptation action. Available materials report dynamic revetment installed, monitoring, adaptive-management activities reported. Site monitoring observations reported, and no universal effect estimate. cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Safer Together bushfire program.
cases.summary: In Victoria, Australia, How Are We Safer Together? is a planning and design initiative. The program uses risk-based fuel management using landscape-scale fire behavior modeling and community values to prioritize where and how to reduce fuels through planned burns or mechanical treatments. Community collaboration: Partnered with local governments and community members to co-design preparedness and response strategies through tailored outreach, local workshops, and shared decision-making. The case addresses wildfire and Smoke. Available materials report the Safer Together program led to more targeted and transparent fuel management across Victoria, reducing bushfire risk while incorporating community values. It improved collaboration between fire agencies, local governments, and residents, resulting in more trusted and effective preparedness efforts. Public-facing dashboards and risk models increased accountability, while behavioral insights research informed tailored strategies to boost household preparedness. The program also advanced understanding of smoke impacts, helping balance risk reduction with public health.
cases.title: How Are We Safer Together?

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Fire Tree bushfire warning-system study.
cases.summary: In Victoria, Australia, The People and the Fire Tree: Co-Designing a Bushfire Early Warning System is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The project used participatory co-design methods through five workshops with residents of a rural, fire-prone community in Victoria. Participants developed two systems: The Fire Tree—a visual tool for tracking fire threat levels—and The People System—a platform integrating official government resources with informal local communication networks. The collaboration involved researchers from Swinburne University’s Centre for Design Innovation and Centre for Social Impact, emphasizing lived experience, local insight, and institutional coordination. The case addresses wildfire and Smoke, Flooding. Available materials report the result was Bushfire, a prototype early-warning platform tailored to local needs and designed to strengthen both formal and informal communication. The project increased residents’ sense of agency and confidence in preparedness while creating a tool that bridges gaps between community response and institutional systems.
cases.title: The People and the Fire Tree: Co-Designing a Bushfire Early Warning System

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for Portland community depaving and urban heat.
cases.summary: In Portland, OR, Quantifying & Visualizing Urban Heat in Portland through Community Depaving is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. Remote sensing and data mapping and collaborated with Depave, a nonprofit that engages communities in converting pavement to green spaces in vulnerable neighborhoods. The case addresses extreme Heat. Available materials report frontline communities identified-Mapped neighborhoods with both high temperature exposure and social vulnerability, emphasizing areas needing urgent attention, Depaving effectiveness-Demonstrated an average reduction of ~1 °F in surface temperature across depaved sites, highlighting quantifiable cooling benefits, and Method development: Validated a replicable approach combining remote sensing and community intervention to assess and mitigate urban heat impacts.
cases.title: Quantifying & Visualizing Urban Heat in Portland through Community Depaving

cases.asset_alt: Archived EPA case-page image retained for internal review of Chicago green infrastructure and extreme heat.
cases.summary: In Chicago, IL, Chicago Uses Green Infrastructure to Reduce Extreme Heat is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program uses climate vulnerability assessment and introduced green roofs, cool roofs (EPA Energy Star standards), and expanded tree canopy via incentives like expedited permits and tax-funded grants. The case addresses extreme Heat, Flooding. Available materials report data-driven targeting led to investments in green and cool infrastructure across the city’s heat-prone zones, Thousands of trees, cool roofs, and green roofs were installed—green roofs now feature on City Hall and commercial buildings, Heat-resilient planning was institutionalized in Chicago’s 2008 Climate Action Plan and Cook County’s Hazard Mitigation strategy, and Increased community awareness and capacity to respond to heat emergencies, especially in at-risk neighborhoods.
cases.title: Chicago Uses Green Infrastructure to Reduce Extreme Heat

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Paris heat adaptation case.
cases.summary: In Paris, France, Adapting Paris: Climate Resilience Strategies in the Face of Rising Temperatures is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program uses paris implemented over 1,300 “cool islands” by combining data-driven heat risk mapping with nature-based and built solutions like shaded parks, water features, and public building access. The initiative prioritized equitable access, aiming to ensure that all residents, especially in vulnerable neighborhoods, were within a 10-minute walk of a cool zone. The case addresses extreme Heat.
cases.title: Adapting Paris: Climate Resilience Strategies in the Face of Rising Temperatures

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Paris Oasis Schoolyard program.
cases.summary: In Paris, France, Paris Oasis Schoolyard Program is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program used a co-design and nature-based approach Paris was able to turn heat-prone, paved schoolyards into cool, green, and accessible spaces. The project utilized community engagement strategies, climate models, and pilot projects, to successfully implement more permeable surfaces, vegetation, and water retention features to reduce urban heat and stormwater runoff within schoolyards. The case addresses extreme Heat. Available materials report dozens of schoolyards across Paris were successfully redesigned and opened to the public, Surface temperatures in OASIS yards were significantly lower compared to traditional schoolyards, Increased awareness and participation among students, teachers, and neighborhood residents, and The program is now being scaled up as a citywide adaptation measure.
cases.title: Paris Oasis Schoolyard Program

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Island County sea-level-rise study.
cases.summary: The Island County Sea Level Rise Strategy Study aimed to enhance flood preparedness and resilience by providing an actionable framework to strengthen the county’s coastlines, infrastructure, and ecosystems in the face of rising seas. A key objective was to integrate adaptation strategies into Shoreline Master Programs and other planning documents, ensuring that technical data translated effectively into policy. The project also focused on developing practical tools, such as vulnerability maps and implementation frameworks, to support local departments in incorporating sea level rise into everyday decision-making. Through collaborative workshops and public outreach, the study grounded its recommendations in both scientific insight and community values using a co-productive approach.
cases.title: Island County Sea Level Rise Strategy Study

cases.asset_alt: University of Maryland case-page image retained for internal review of the Pines on the Severn living shoreline.
cases.summary: In Arnold, Maryland, Pines on the Severn Living Shoreline is an implementation initiative. The documented approach is to construct a 400-foot living shoreline rather than replacing failing bulkheads with hard shoreline reinforcement. Shoreline erosion, flooding, drainage, and runoff pressures affected the community's shared Severn River waterfront. The original source reports increased usable waterfront acreage, improved aesthetics and wildlife habitat, and greater resident awareness of water-quality issues.
cases.title: Pines on the Severn Living Shoreline

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for the Powell Shoreline Restoration Project.
cases.summary: In Bainbridge Island, WA, Powell Shoreline Restoration Project is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The documented approach is to remove bulkheads and Employ soft shoreline stabilization techniques. The case addresses marine and Coastal Changes. Available materials report initiated in 2009 as a community-driven collaboration between the Powel family, Bainbridge Island Land Trust, and state and federal salmon recovery funders, the project removed approximately one-third of a mile of aging bulkheads and over 1,340 tons of riprap, concrete, and creosote timber. Over 2,500 native plants were installed, invasive species cleared, and intertidal habitat expanded by roughly 163%. A diverse stakeholder group—ranging from tribal representatives to city, engineering, and ecological experts guided the design process, supported by 1,200+ volunteer hours. The project also restored intertidal and salt marsh habitat, benefiting salmon and other wildlife.
cases.title: Powell Shoreline Restoration Project

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for Seattle Public Schools geothermal systems.
cases.summary: In Seattle, WA, Geothermal Heat Pump Case Study: Seattle Public Schools is an implementation initiative. The program uses geo-thermal heat pumps and electric boilers. The case addresses extreme Heat and Public Health. Available materials report all schools involved in project have replaced gas-fired boilers with geothermal heat pumps and electric boilers. Seattle Public Schools’ electrical supply is 91% renewable, and carbon credits offset the remaining 9%, and operational greenhouse gas emissions are minimal.
cases.title: Geothermal Heat Pump Case Study: Seattle Public Schools

cases.summary: In San Francisco, CA, San Francisco – Drought Resilience Matrix is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program uses internal planning tool, cross-departmental use. The case addresses drought and Water Supply. Available materials report the creation of the Drought Resilience Matrix to evaluate water supply alternatives in Urban Areas, and The study concluded that while no solution is perfect, local, diversified supply options tend to be the most robust under prolonged drought conditions.
cases.title: San Francisco – Drought Resilience Matrix

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for San Diego Gas and Electric wildfire operations.
cases.summary: In San Diego, CA, San Diego Gas & Electric Wildfire Strategy is a monitoring and adaptive management initiative. The program used inter-organizational collaboration between SDG&E, UCLA, and the U.S. Forest Service a multidisciplinary tool was developed to aid in wildfire response and mitigation: Santa Ana Wildfire Threat Index. The case addresses wildfire and Smoke. Available materials report improved forecasts of fire-conducive weather, especially during Santa Ana events, with several days of advance notice. Operational enhancements, like temporarily disabling trunk lines in vulnerable areas, reducing the chance of equipment sparking fires. Cost savings, through avoided damages, reduced outages, and fewer wildfire ignitions linked to power infrastructure. Enhanced public safety, thanks to earlier alerts and better-prepared firefighters and utility staff.
cases.title: San Diego Gas & Electric Wildfire Strategy

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for invasive plants under climate change.
cases.summary: The primary goal of the Northwest RISCC Network project was to assess and address how climate change may increase the risk posed by invasive plant species in the Pacific Northwest. As temperatures rise and ecosystems shift, some non-native species that were previously benign or regionally constrained may become invasive threats. The project aimed to help land managers, policymakers, and regulatory agencies prepare for these changes by identifying high-risk species and adapting management tools and regulations accordingly.
cases.title: Risks & Regulation of Invasive Plants in a Changing Climate

cases.asset_alt: Image retained from the existing CIG case entry for Yakama Nation restoration and cultural knowledge.
cases.summary: This project will remove two diversion dams and a non-functional fish screen and replace them with appropriate fish passage structures on the Toppenish Creek in Washington. Removing these barriers will provide a clearer migration path to spawning habitats for Pacific lamprey and threatened steelhead. In addition to the benefits for fish species, this project will restore and enhance more than 450 acres of wetland habitat on the floodplain of Toppenish Creek. These floodplain wetlands are invaluable wildlife habitat for both migratory and resident species. Toppenish Creek is culturally significant to the Yakama Nation and the area serves as an educational site to retain tribal culture. Yakama Tribal members also hunt on the properties, and gather traditional foods and materials such as Wapato, tule, currants and chokecherries, and willow and dogwood.
cases.title: Natural Restoration and Cultural Knowledge of the Yakama Nation
